429b68e56684.text: Why education belongs in the project

bd6599350f72.text: A decision has to be practised.

c38b4014b3d9.text: Education is a right, and a way for people to take part in decisions that affect them. Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and SDG 4 give that commitment a public foundation; Target 4.7 connects learning to sustainable development. For AeroSense, it means making the science accessible enough to question, use and eventually build on.

d5e3e4c250f7.text: Our initial survey changed the question we wanted to ask. Explaining that mold can be dangerous was too broad. Our working summary pointed instead to decisions people make about heat, smell and visible spoilage. We therefore built opportunities to choose an answer, see why it matters and try a new situation. The team now reports 107 responses; item-level counts still need verification, so this page does not turn the early summary into population percentages.

5432ac2be556.text: Active participation gave us a useful starting point. Freeman and colleagues' synthesis of 225 undergraduate STEM studies found an average 0.47-standard-deviation improvement in examination performance with active learning. Wouters and colleagues found benefits of serious games for learning and retention, with no clear overall motivation advantage. Those results justify testing an approach; they do not establish that our own games work.

0eb9944632a3.text: We also wanted a conversation about synthetic biology itself. What does it mean to put a fruit-fly odor receptor into cultured HEK293 cells? What can a fluorescent response tell us? Who should act on a screening result? Each activity below gives a different audience a way into those questions.

The biological circuit has feedback and parallel pathways; the map is a reading guide.

b96b117de2d2.text: Disagree. Appearance and smell cannot establish mycotoxin status. Absence of an off-odor does not prove absence of toxin; presence of mold does not by itself quantify a toxin. Sensory inspection is not an assay.

Article 26 states that everyone has the right to education, that it shall be free at least in the elementary and fundamental stages, and that it "shall be directed to the full development of the human personality and to the strengthening of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms"

ed77381620b2.text: Information alone does not ensure behavior change. Research challenges the "deficit model" that treats mistaken views as simply a lack of facts: knowledge and attitudes have a more complex relationship [3], and scientists' training and assumptions about audiences can sustain that model [4]. Pro-environmental research likewise identifies a gap between knowing and doing [5].

68bc7b0d5cf5.text: Access to information is not the same as education that changes what people do. Science-communication research has long questioned the "deficit model", the assumption that people hold mistaken views because they lack facts. Knowledge does shape attitudes, but the relationship is far more nuanced than the model assumes

3dbdba86cd74.text: , and the model persists for reasons that include how scientists are trained and how they imagine their audiences

ab90548ce8b6.text: . Research on pro-environmental behavior documents the same distance between knowing and doing

d96a1cae1e57.text: Our survey found a similar gap: only 58% understood that normal appearance and smell do not rule out risk, and higher knowledge did not consistently translate into action. We therefore looked to active learning. Across 225 science, engineering and mathematics studies, it improved exam performance by 0.47 standard deviations and reduced failure rates to 21.8%, compared with 33.8% [6]. A serious-games meta-analysis found benefits for learning (d = 0.29) and retention (d = 0.36), but not motivation [7]. These formal-course findings guide our design; our own activities still need evaluation with their intended audiences.

72318d9e2d81.text: Our own survey pointed the same way. Most respondents already understood that visible mold is a problem, so a lecture saying "mold is dangerous" would have repeated what many people knew. The gap was in the risks that cannot be seen: only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk, and even respondents with higher knowledge often did not act on it. We went looking for what the research suggests works instead: active learning raised exam performance by 0.47 standard deviations and lowered failure rates (21.8% against 33.8%) across 225 science, engineering, and mathematics studies

5b6601f70a01.text: , and in a meta-analysis of serious-games studies, serious games outperformed conventional instruction on learning (d = 0.29) and retention (d = 0.36), though they were not more motivating

fd4d57b073e6.text: Biological meaning. The antennal lobe is the fly's primary olfactory processing center — roughly 50 anatomically distinct glomeruli, each wired to a single receptor type, where signal from thousands of olfactory sensory neurons first converges. Nothing is interpreted yet here; it's simply where every receptor channel's raw reading arrives in parallel. It's the literal starting point of "a smell is a pattern across many channels" — the idea our whole sensing platform, and Module 1 (Discover) of our online Learning Lab, is built on.

8102997156fd.text: How we reach this stage of education. We treat the AL as our broadest-reach layer. None of the three projects here are trying to teach anyone anything in depth — they're trying to find out what the widest possible audience already believes (Public Survey), get them to make a decision and see its consequence in under fifteen minutes (Online Games), or keep the same corrective claim in front of them through feeds, short videos, and articles they already read (Social Media, Short Video & Articles). Like the AL itself, breadth comes before interpretation.

63c8f8afca1c.text: Before designing activities, we asked what people believed about mold and mycotoxin risk, and whether that knowledge shaped their storage habits. The survey let us test the knowledge gap rather than assume it.

c4541ffaa128.text: We ran a bilingual (Chinese and English) online questionnaire on mold and mycotoxin understanding, food-storage habits and what people want from a screening tool. It reached 300 respondents. Three findings shaped the rest of our education work:

90df4ac4d827.text: Public understanding varies by risk concept. People were most secure about the risk they can see. 78% understood that removing visible mold does not always make food safe. Understanding was lower for heat, where 64% understood that heating does not always destroy all mycotoxins, and lowest for looks and smell, where only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk. On that last item 27% were unsure and 15% held the misconception. The risks that cannot be seen are the ones people understand least, and they are the risks our sensor is meant to address.

23b054009155.text: Knowledge does not automatically translate into practice. We compared respondents with higher knowledge (n = 180) with those with lower or uncertain knowledge (n = 120). Higher-knowledge respondents were more likely to record the opening date (42% against 25%) and to report a recommended storage practice (71% against 46%). But even in the higher-knowledge group, 58% did not record the opening date. Knowing the facts helped, but it did not close the gap between knowing and doing.

2329b765700f.text: Users value trustworthy, actionable results. Asked what they need from a screening tool, respondents chose trustworthiness of results (76%) and accuracy, including avoiding false negatives (73%) first, followed by clear next-step guidance (68%). These ranked ahead of ease of use (61%), affordable cost per test (54%) and a fast result (49%). People do not only want a number; they want to trust it and know what to do next.

26770da7897b.text: The survey shaped three design choices. Games and Learning Lab Module 2 focus on the limits of heat, appearance and smell, using the same statements as the survey for later comparison. Lessons and posts add practical habits such as recording opening dates. The Learning Lab also explains the limits of screening and what to do next, while our design prioritizes avoiding missed risk.

0b8b551ddb8a.text: These are self-reported answers from people who chose to respond, so they show where to look, not how common each belief or habit is across Taiwan.

e18333032382.text: The survey revealed decisions to practise: recording when a package was opened instead of relying only on its printed date, and judging the limits of heat and smell tests. We designed a game in which learners make those decisions and see their consequences, connecting the education loop to the project's motivation.

ff47d00de7a8.text: Series 1: From fly nose to edge device.

222c36f7587d.text: Three posts that follow one smell through the AeroSense system, one post per layer: the living sensor, the decoding model, and the hardware. Each post is a short carousel written for readers with no biology or engineering background.

4c98f1094956.text: Post 1, Parts Design: "We put a fruit fly's nose inside a human cell." Explains how a fruit fly odor receptor and a calcium-sensitive glow protein, placed in human cells, turn a smell into light: an odor molecule binds the receptor, calcium flows in, and the cell lights up. The brighter the glow, the stronger the smell.

cfbf83b0a402.text: Post 2, Model: "The cell lit up. Now what?" How a circuit modeled on the fruit fly brain turns the glow into a decision. Coming soon.

e9eccf3c593a.text: Post 3, Hardware: "Hearing a cell's faint glow in a noisy room." How the edge device picks a faint signal out of background noise.

025a930e1335.text: Four multiple-choice Instagram stories, each followed by an answer card. Every question ties one AeroSense design choice to a Sustainable Development Goal, so followers learn what the goals mean by guessing which one applies.

a1b8d8d52917.text: Flagging a batch of bananas or mangoes before disease symptoms are visible points to SDG 2, Zero Hunger. An edge classifier under 1 W, with core logic from a paper our own team published, points to SDG 9, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure. A reusable, non-destructive sensing cartridge points to SDG 12, Responsible Consumption and Production. And the interviews with an e-nose company's chief scientist, several biotech companies, and an analytical-instrumentation professor point to SDG 17, Partnerships for the Goals.

16396d9b786e.text: Impact on us. We treat social media as a reach channel, not a measurement tool. Over the posting period, our feed posts reached more than 1,700 accounts, our stories more than 1,400, and our reels more than 500, with an average of about 50 likes per post. We gained more than 100 new followers, and more than 50 people answered the Sustainability Pop Quiz stories, getting about 75% correct on average. Our best-performing post was Post 2, "The cell lit up. Now what?" Most of our audience was aged 20 to 30.

c3a68dd410c2.text: These numbers show interest, not learning. Saves, poll responses, and comment questions cannot tell us whether someone understood an idea, so we measure knowledge change where we can pair a before and an after: in the game and the Learning Lab. Our own observation from comparable in-person outreach, such as street booths and pub-quiz events, is that this kind of content tends to over-index on audiences who are already interested in science. The age data does not settle this, because it tells us who followed, not whether they were already interested in science.

87d234b0cd1a.text: The calyx is the dendritic input zone of the mushroom body — around 2,000 Kenyon cells receive sparse, combinatorial input here from antennal-lobe projection neurons, and this is where parallel receptor channels actually get bound together into one learnable, associative pattern. It's the integration step — the subject of Module 4 (Decode) of our curriculum — and biologically, it's where exposure becomes memory.

7029bb71c5d1.text: How we reach this stage of education.

3342e19c0915.text: The three projects here have a different job than the first part's: they're not trying to reach as many people as possible, they're trying to turn a shorter exposure into real, structured understanding, across the full age range our work touches — elementary schoolers, university life-science and medical students, and a self-paced option open to anyone.

a565a50dcefd.text: Shan-chi Elementary School is a rural school in Xinfeng Township, Hsinchu County. Bringing a hands-on science session to a school there is a small step toward the equal access to quality education that SDG 4 describes. The camp also lets us test our claim that the game can be understood by children, instead of assuming it.

a387dc17d67f.text: On October 12, 2026 we ran a half-day science camp at the school for more than thirty upper-grade pupils (grades 5 and 6).

d2b928ca0ac1.text: We started with a Science Mini-Class. In about ten minutes we asked three questions in a row: How does a nose smell? How does an electronic nose smell? And what does our lab do? Each answer built on the one before, so the children could follow a smell from their own nose, to a machine, to the sensor we are building.

007801065b32.text: Next, the children played Odor Pixel Suite, the game we designed, as a challenge that lasted about ten minutes. We adapted it for a whole class. Instead of one child at one screen, the questions were projected on a screen, and each team answered at the same time by holding up one, two, or three fingers.

5a2363f0c517.text: Then came a drawing and worksheet session of about fifteen minutes. The children drew a cartoon nose or a cartoon fruit fly, and completed a worksheet. The children's drawings are shown in the Art Exhibition section below.

2c0cd1693e88.text: We collected 22 worksheets from the camp, each asking what the child learned or felt. Thirteen children named something they had learned, and nine wrote only that they had fun or liked the game. Five wrote about the electronic nose, and five mentioned the game. One wrote that the memory game was "really hard," and another noted that it had "a lot of questions."

4cd597c61eb3.text: Several children put the science in their own words. One wrote that everyday smells are made of many tiny molecules. Another wrote that different animals smell in different ways and that smelling uses the brain, not only the nose. A third wrote that we can use the brain in place of the nose. One wrote that technology is powerful and should be used to build the future, and one asked the school to hold the activity again.

91579a58b0ac.text: This suggests that children could follow the path from nose to electronic nose and enjoyed the game, although the worksheets are short and self-reported, so they do not measure how much each child understood.

a0227eb37857.text: 2. Olfactory Neuroscience Workshop (with Prof. Chung-Chuan Lo)

e343ccb1970e.text: The workshop connected olfactory neuroscience to our sensor design: how a brain turns smell into a decision, and how that logic informs an electronic nose. It also gave us a first chance to assess the full sequence of talk, project and online activities with students approaching a field choice.

1403dfe99586.text: On October 14, 2026, we ran "From the Brain to the Electronic Nose," a workshop for students of the NTHU College of Life Science and Medicine. Prof. Lo then spoke on the biological logic underneath olfaction: how receptors bind odor molecules, how a single smell is represented by a combination of receptors rather than one, and how the fly's antennal lobe and mushroom body turn that pattern into a decision. He also showed how this circuit-level understanding from computational neuroscience has inspired approaches to artificial intelligence.

cdd683f5a562.text: We followed with introducing our project: why early detection of food mold and crop disease matters, how a living-cell sensor built from an olfactory receptor and a fluorescent reporter detects volatile compounds, and how a fly-brain-inspired classifier reads the resulting "odor fingerprint." We closed that part with the idea that how biology smells is how we design. Then everyone tried our online platform. We gave a short tour of the Learning Lab, running one module live so that students could see how its five modules fit together. The workshop ended with a feedback form.

7ceeaae39371.text: The workshop drew 15 participants, split evenly across doctoral, master's, and bachelor's students. Prof. Lo's talk received the highest satisfaction, and participants strongly agreed that they understood the olfactory mechanism and the electronic nose mechanism better after attending.

b3167191574f.text: Their suggestions were specific. Some English technical terms were hard to follow, which made it difficult to understand the rest of the talk, remember where a term had appeared, and ask questions afterward. Participants wanted a take-home message that gives the overall picture of the project, and asked us to explain the neural network, the project goal, and the intended use more clearly.

21f53f037a9f.text: 3. AeroSense Learning Lab — the online curriculum

9517f5360834.text: The Learning Lab extends access beyond a camp or workshop, so learning does not depend on living near a university. At their own pace from home, learners can follow how a fly smells, how a living cell becomes a sensor, and what a screening result can and cannot tell them about food safety.

The modules can be taken in any order, but they are designed to follow the logic of the project itself, as listed below.

2badbd5f342e.text: Discover. How animals smell: receptors binding odor molecules, and sparse, combinatorial coding in the fly antennal lobe and mushroom body.

1b82361a014d.text: Question. Mold versus mycotoxin risk, and why looks and smell cannot be trusted.

d0613bb467af.text: Build. Expressing OR/Orco and GCaMP6 in cultured cells to make a self-renewing living sensor.

955cf1e4c64c.text: Decode. A smell as a pattern across many receptors, and how fly-brain-inspired computation reads it.

0dfb21c46698.text: Decide. Screening is not certified testing: risk tiers and the correct next action.

46988d0d4ea4.text: Each module ends with three check questions. The full set is in the teacher toolkit, described under Teacher Toolkit & Education Guide in Mushroom Body Lobes / MBON.

1b52edecaf0c.text: More than 500 people have gone through the Learning Lab. Because Module 2 reuses the survey's statements word for word, their answers can be compared with our survey baseline of 300 respondents.

f7b3dc55c665.text: Learners told us two things, and we changed the platform in response. First, the interface was unclear and the opening had too much text, so we cut the text and separated sections with color blocks to make the page easier to follow. Second, the opening was too difficult. To make the platform accessible to more people, we lowered the difficulty of the opening and closing sections and added hands-on tasks, so that learners understand by doing.

7ac9ae009130.text: Mushroom Body Lobes / MBON: output (validation and handover)

73d949b430e7.text: Kenyon cell axons run through the mushroom body lobes, where mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) read the learned pattern and convert it into an actual decision — approach or avoid. It's the output stage — the subject of Module 5 (Decide) of our online Learning Lab — and biologically, it's where internal learning becomes visible, external behavior.

66822acaacd7.text: The projects here aren't about reach or depth — they're about what happens when our work gets read out to an outside expert audience and has to hold up: an industry conference, a peer iGEM team, and an academic lecture hall. It also holds the two ways our work leaves the room: a toolkit other teachers can run, and an exhibition of what participants made.

1dd5119a5979.text: SynBioBeta let us learn from practicing synthetic biologists, founders and investors through the Next-Gen BioLeaders community. At the poster session, we tested whether a mixed, non-specialist audience could understand our central idea in a few minutes: a smell is a pattern read by a fly-inspired circuit.

2dc9a513a92a.text: At SynBioBeta 2026 (San Jose, May 4 to 7), as one of the Next-Gen BioLeaders, with our poster accepted and presented in the Expo Hall. The poster, "Development of a Bionic Olfactory Edge Computing System Integrating Drosophila Neural Models and Live-Cell Sensor Arrays," fit the whole platform on one page for a mixed audience: why conventional electronic noses fall short, how the fly solves the problem, and why we use living cells.

72d7f5c6a4b3.text: The poster showed us where the explanation broke. A PhD student from UCLA, with a wet-lab background, told us he had not known how a live-cell sensor is actually built. That was the step we had explained least.

fbe844fdf355.text: The hardest question we were asked was whether our living-cell system can scale. Two more followed: how a medically positioned device would be regulated, and whether the hardware has enough margin. They came from people who evaluate companies, not student projects.

516cfa12cc83.text: Our formal Human Practices work had not yet begun in May, so this was our first read on the project from outside the lab, and the questions landed on the wet lab, the model and the hardware. They changed our plan and led us to add consultations. The scale question led to state the concrete follow-up, such as a cartridge-lifetime test or a consultation on cell production. The regulatory question led us to add regulatory consultation and to move our first application from medical diagnostics to agriculture, where the path to market is more accessible.

49cd8ad3003a.text: The poster's wording changed with the plan. The April poster lists medical point-of-care testing, including non-invasive breath diagnostics, alongside agriculture and environmental monitoring; our current materials present AeroSense as an agricultural and food-safety screening platform.

99d01144fad9.text: Other iGEM teams could assess both our research and our education work. The cross-border meeting offered technical criticism from experienced peers and a chance to compare how teams teach.

e7940b7e5a5c.text: On October 8, 2026, iGEM TAU-Israel hosted an online Mini Jamboree. Eight teams from six countries took part: NCKU-Tainan and NTHU from Taiwan, CAU-China and AIS-China from China, CERNAL from Israel, Cell Forge from India, iGEM-UA Alicante from Spain, and UFRGS-Brazil. Each team presented for about fifteen minutes, so every team heard seven other projects and every project was heard by teams in different regions with different regulations, farming and school systems. Besides our project, we also shared the education work described on this page, so that our activities could be compared with theirs.

56b57723ec36.text: The circuit our classifier is built on comes from research co-published by our advisor, Prof. Chung-Chuan Lo, and Prof. Ching-Che Charng of China Medical University (Cheng et al., Science Advances, 2025). Prof. Charng invited us to bring that shared research back to his university, to an audience that could judge how we had used it.

7c4ffd5b35a4.text: On September 23, 2026, a member of our model team gave a research-sharing lecture on our electronic-nose work to more than thirty undergraduate and graduate students at China Medical University. The lecture followed one thread: why electronic noses drift and why recalibrating them is costly; how the insect olfactory system keeps its odor code stable; and how our spiking neural network borrows those ideas. We also presented the results that do not flatter the model: the 14 sensors in our test dataset behave like only three types, adding more features did not help once the data had been compressed, and accuracy fell to about 75% when odors were presented continuously. We taught the evidence together with its limits so that listeners could judge the method themselves.

a5bc9f5a00b4.text: Most of the audience's questions were about how the model processes an odor: how sensor readings become a pattern, and how that pattern becomes a decision. They showed us that this step needs a plainer explanation than we had given. We changed how we introduced the model in the olfactory neuroscience workshop that followed.

06d1225abee2.text: We asked participants of the elementary school science camp, the olfactory neuroscience workshop and other activities to draw "the electronic nose and the fruit fly as you imagine them," and we treat their drawings as a creative output of our education work. What a learner draws shows what they took away in their own terms, which a quiz cannot show. The drawings are displayed on our Art Gallery page

8324883ca9d7.text: 5. Teacher Toolkit & Education Guide — open resources

2cb3fc87428a.text: Teacher Toolkit. When we met the principal of the elementary school where we ran our science camp, he told us he liked the way we teach and asked for a way to keep using it, since we cannot visit every year. We packaged the camp into a teacher toolkit: the lesson slides, the Odor Pixel Suite game, and instructions for using the Learning Lab, so that a teacher can run the same session without us. The school welcomed the approach, and the toolkit is free for any teacher to download.

2dc53d9ab92b.text: Education Guide. The Education Guide is written for other teams, as a PDF on our Contribution page. It sets out the steps we followed: find out what your audience believes, choose one claim, match the format to the audience, measure the same way each time, and hand the work on, so that a team that has never met us can plan its own education work.

8aef70293bbc.text: Testing our initial assumption identified a narrower teaching need: most respondents knew mold was dangerous, but some still trusted heat, appearance or smell to judge safety. Our activities carry that testable claim from first contact (Region 1), through structured learning (Region 2), to outside feedback and handover (Region 3).

2066953b9fb2.text: The antennal lobe is the fly's primary olfactory processing center — roughly 50 anatomically distinct glomeruli, each wired to a single receptor type, where signal from thousands of olfactory sensory neurons first converges. Nothing is interpreted yet here; it's simply where every receptor channel's raw reading arrives in parallel. It's the literal starting point of "a smell is a pattern across many channels" — the idea our whole sensing platform, and Module 1 (Discover) of our online Learning Lab, is built on.

42bf775e46cf.text: We treat the AL as our broadest-reach layer. None of the three projects here are trying to teach anyone anything in depth — they're trying to find out what the widest possible audience already believes (Public Survey), get them to make a decision and see its consequence in under fifteen minutes (Online Games), or keep the same corrective claim in front of them through feeds, short videos, and articles they already read (Social Media, Short Video & Articles). Like the AL itself, breadth comes before interpretation.
